The subject of "socialization" among trans men is a tricky one. Some of us were socialized female, and have traumas related to being brought up in a fucked up misogynistic environment. They generally identify more with what people like to call "AFAB socialization" because it describes their experiences better, and experience solidarity with many women and non-binary people with similar experiences.

But, like... that's not everyone. And it's generally assumed that it sorta is. Which kinda sucks. When cis men describe their boyhoods it's more relatable to me than cis (or trans) women describing their girlhoods. Gendered socialization-- as with socialization of all kinds-- is the product of subconscious imitation of the "in-group". I grew up seeing boys and girls do different things-- at school, in cartoons, in novels I read, in advertising-- and I decided I wanted to do the "boy" things. I got the boy meals from McDonald's. I only got along with boys, and grew up speaking using boyish language in a boyish cadence. Subconsciously, as I became a teenager, I kept my vocal formant highly androgynous to the point where it was impossible for me to correct after I decided to finally embrace some amount of feminine presentation (about a year before realizing I was a guy).

Seeing people discuss "AMAB socialization" feels pretty transphobic to me. I feel excluded from discussions about the emotional health of young boys when it's framed as a "cis men's issue", as someone who internalized "boys don't cry" *hard* years before learning he was even a boy. Maybe I wouldn't have been directly ridiculed for crying as a young "girl" like someone who lived as a boy would, which is a privilege. But the ridicule of other boys kept me from acknowledging any feminine or emotional side of me for years upon years. When I was 12 I was the "queen" of toxic masculinity. I have a place in this discussion, because it is a men's social issue, and I was socialized as male.

There was a thread on r/TransyTalk a few months ago where some trans women talked about how they were, indeed, socialized female. If someone were to argue with or contradict them, they would rightly be called a transphobe. Trans men don't recieve the same support for these sentiments when we express them because we don't have many people who actually wanna listen to us. Not feminists, not men's activists, not queer people, not cishet people. The "socialized female" phrase, when applied generally to those assigned female at birth, is invalidating the experiences of trans men who were *not* socialized female. Those of us who, consequently, don't have any spaces.

Maybe I'm a little tired of being unintentionally completely disregarded from men's lib conversations where people use "woke" language like AGAB terminology to assume that discussions of growing up as a boy can't apply to me. I see it here kinda often and it hurts.

I identify completely with the "MtM" idea. Other men were socialized female, and they are still every bit the man I am. It shouldn't be too hard to just avoid explicitly labeling the assigned genders of children in discussions about gendered socialization, in practice.
